quote: Man suche in der complexen x Ebene diejenigen Punkte für welche 2 Werthe der Function y dem abso- luten Betrage nach gleich sind.
english: One should find in the complex x-plane those points for which 2 values of the function y are equal in absolute value.
topic: Notes on applying Chebyshev's methods to numbers, a plan to axiomatize mechanics and other physics like geometry, and a problem about points in the complex x-plane where two values of an algebraic function have equal absolute value.

triage.modern_statement: Let y(x) be an algebraic function, F(x,y)=0, with branches y_1(x),...,y_n(x). Describe the set of points x in C where two branches have the same modulus, |y_i(x)| = |y_j(x)| for some i ≠ j. Today this set is called the 'equimodular' locus. Away from branch points it is locally a real-analytic curve, given by Re(log y_i − log y_j) = 0, and it can be cut out by real-algebraic equations in Re x and Im x. Hilbert wrote no aim or context, so his reason for asking cannot be recovered.
triage.answered_by: There is no single solution to Hilbert's note, and no source links it to him. The object itself, the equimodular curve of the branches of an algebraic function, became standard and well understood. Its key role was set out by S. Beraha, J. Kahane and N. J. Weiss (1978; Zbl 0477.05034). Their theorem says that zeros of sequences of the form sum_j alpha_j(x) lambda_j(x)^n, where the lambda_j are branches of an algebraic function such as transfer-matrix eigenvalues, collect on the curves where two dominant branches have equal modulus. Later papers give explicit equations and structure results for these curves, e.g. 'Extension to the Beraha-Kahane-Weiss Theorem' and recent papers giving explicit equimodular curves for prism-graph chromatic polynomials.

evidence.claim: The Beraha–Kahane–Weiss theorem says the zeros approach the curves where the matrix has two eigenvalues of equal modulus, and these 'equimodular' curves are studied in their own right.
Under BKW, roots collect where two dominant branches have equal modulus, which gives continuous accumulation curves, plus isolated points where a dominant amplitude vanishes.
Recent work gives closed real-algebraic (Cartesian quartic) equations for such modulus-tie sets, e.g. |z^2-3z+3| = |z-1|.
Equimodular curves of transfer-matrix eigenvalues, which are branches of an algebraic function, are used to study the zeros of the hard-hexagon partition function at complex fugacity.

triage.why: The note is one line with no context. As a general task it is fairly routine: the locus |y_i| = |y_j| can be written down by elimination as a real-algebraic set. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source connecting it to Hilbert or saying he followed it up. The same object, the equimodular curve of algebraic-function branches, did become central later. Since Beraha–Kahane–Weiss (1978) it explains where zeros of chromatic polynomials and partition functions accumulate, and papers on it still appeared in 2020–2026, so the area is active. The verdict 'solved' means only that this kind of locus is now well understood. It does not mean anyone answered Hilbert's note. His purpose (for example convergence of series, uniformization, or which branch dominates) is unknown, so confidence is low.
